newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--US housing start slide seen ended in Nov.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--US housing start slide seen ended in Nov.

text.p: A two-month slide in U.S. housing starts likely came to a halt in November, and lower mortgage rates may soon spark an uptrend, economists said Friday.
For September and October combined, housing starts fell 11.2 percent to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.366 million -- the lowest rate since 1.351 million in October 1995.
The November data, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT Tuesday, are widely expected to show a mild rebound, but economists were wary of calling it the start of an upturn.

"I see a leveling off but I don't see a reversal of trend," said Peter Kretzmer, economist at NationsBank Corp. His preliminary forecast is for a November rate of 1.39 million starts, up slightly from the October level.
"We saw above-trend housing growth in the first half of the year," he said. But a weakening trend set in during the summer.
Changes in housing starts tend to lag changes in mortgage rates, so the rise in rates in the first half of the year was partially responsible for the October-September slide, economists said.
The drop in rates in the second half is expected to aid the housing sector in coming months, they said.

"Rates have come down quite a bit in the last month or two and housing does react with a lag...," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc. He forecast a slight rebound in November housing starts, to an annual rate of 1.42 million.
"If starts continue to fall, despite the fall in interest rates, then we have to start thinking there is something slightly more seriously wrong in the economy than a slight pullback," Low said.
Cheryl Katz, senior economist at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc, also forecast a modest rebound in housing starts in November, to an annual rate of 1.40 million.

While economists were hesitant to say November represented the start of a reversal of the two-month downtrend, many were confident that a pick-up in housing would be seen in the first quarter of 1997.
